Big O notation. A mathematical framework for describing how a function's value grows relative to its input size. In computer science, it quantifies algorithm efficiency by expressing the worst-case time or space resources as input approaches infinity. Big O strips away constant factors and lower-order terms, revealing the dominant growth pattern: linear, quadratic, logarithmic, or exponential. It is the lingua franca of algorithm analysis.

Big O formalizes "grows no faster than." If there exist constants c and n zero such that f of n is less than or equal to c times g of n for all n greater than or equal to n zero, then f of n equals O of g of n. The notation ignores constant factors and lower-order terms. For example, two n plus five simplifies to O of n, and n squared plus n plus seven simplifies to O of n squared. Big O measures worst-case behavior, the most resource-intensive input of a given size.

The common complexity classes span from constant O of one for hash table lookups and array access, to logarithmic O of log n for binary search and balanced tree insertion, linear O of n for array scans, and linearithmic O of n log n for optimal sorting algorithms like merge sort. Quadratic O of n squared appears in nested-loop algorithms like bubble sort. Cubic O of n cubed shows up in naive matrix multiplication. Exponential O of two to the n applies to brute-force subset enumeration, while factorial O of n factorial applies to generating all permutations.

Big O allows rigorous algorithm comparison independent of hardware or language. It predicts scalability: O of n scales to large inputs, while O of two to the n hits a wall quickly. At n equals forty, that is ten to the twelfth operations. Space complexity uses the same notation. An algorithm might be O of n time and O of one space, or O of n time and O of n space.

There are related notations beyond Big O. Big omega gives a lower bound, formalizing "grows no slower than." Big theta gives a tight bound, meaning f and g have the same asymptotic growth. Little o means f grows strictly slower than g.

Big O notation is foundational because it abstracts away physical details of computation—CPU speed, memory latency, cache behavior—and focuses on intrinsic algorithmic cost. When your input size doubles, knowing whether an algorithm's running time doubles, quadruples, or stays almost the same is the difference between a responsive system and one that grinds to a halt. Big O has become standard in job interviews, algorithm courses, and engineering decisions.
